subjects.name: The Man-Plant, or a Scheme for Increasing and Improving the British Breed

summary: Lincolnshire-born Thomas Thistlewood went to Jamaica in 1750, rose from overseer to plantation owner, and spent 36 years recording in his diaries the rapes, floggings and tortures he inflicted on the people he enslaved.

evidence.note: birth in Lincolnshire in 1721 and father's death in 1727 open the biography
1746 East India Company voyage as purser; covered briefly, so no Asian setting added
arrives in Jamaica in May 1750 and starts as bookkeeper and assistant overseer
segment on island demographics and why poor whites were courted by planters
first recorded sexual assault on an enslaved woman, coded in Latin, begins long analysis
long segment on the 1752 satirical tract The Man-Plant and its proto-eugenic ideas
detailed account of plantation punishments: pickling, branding, Derby's dose
buys his own 160-acre property in 1767 after years renting out enslaved workers
account of Bess, bought at eleven and later abused, supports child-abuse
death in 1786 at sixty-five; abolition aftermath only a short coda

notes: No role for slaveholder or planter; colonial-administrator (settler who profited from a colony) plus business-executive is the closest fit, criminal-killer for the documented rapes and torture. The Man-Plant author is pseudonymous (Vincent Miller), so the book is the secondary subject. Phibbah, Eve and Bess appear often but are victims, not separate segments.
